Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "North Window Audio will release “The Last Ferry Bell,” a 52-minute episode of its independent radio drama *Harbor Lights*, on October 18. The story follows Mara Venn, a night dispatcher at the fictional Bellwether ferry terminal, during the final crossing of the season. A storm has closed the eastern route, a relief crew is delayed by a road closure, and the terminal’s old signal bell rings twice after the last scheduled departure. The episode was written by Celia Marr and directed by Rowan Pike. North Window Audio will publish it on its website and through the usual podcast feeds at 6 a.m. Eastern time.

The production uses a cast of six performers and was recorded over three sessions in a small studio in Portland, Maine. Inez Vale voices Mara, while Graham Holt plays ferry captain Ellis Rook. The other roles are performed by Nadiya Chen, Peter Lyle, Simone Dyer, and Theo Grant. A cast member also reads the brief harbor notices heard between scenes. The script includes a short exchange in English and French, with both lines translated in the episode transcript. No outside narrator introduces the story; information about the storm and the terminal emerges through radio calls, a maintenance log, and conversations in the dispatch room.

Pike said the production team wanted the ferry terminal to feel busy without making the dialogue difficult to follow. “We kept the room sounds close and specific,” Pike said. “You can hear the ticket printer, the heater catching, and the metal latch on Mara’s window. Those small sounds tell you where she is, even when the radio traffic gets crowded.” The sound design includes recorded rain from a public pier, a manually operated signal bell, and a low motor effect built from two separate recordings. The team made the bell sound in the studio rather than using the real Bellwether terminal’s signal, which is not part of the fictional setting.

Marr based the episode’s schedule on the operating patterns of small coastal ferries, but Bellwether and its routes are invented. The script does not identify a precise year. Its references to printed manifests, handheld radios, and a computer in the ticket office were chosen to leave the period open. “I wanted the equipment to feel familiar but not pin the story to one decade,” Marr said. “The important clock is the one the crew is watching before the last boat leaves.” The episode’s main action takes place during roughly ninety minutes, although recorded calls briefly refer to events earlier in the day.

The release includes an accessible transcript, a cast list, and a production note describing the sound effects. The transcript identifies speakers and marks the short French exchange with an English translation. It does not include every environmental sound, but it labels cues that affect the action, including the two bell rings and the terminal announcement that the eastern route is closed. North Window Audio says listeners can download the transcript as a tagged PDF or read it on the episode page. The production note also distinguishes recorded effects from sounds made during the studio sessions.

1. Episode details

Title: “The Last Ferry Bell”
Series: *Harbor Lights*
Written by: Celia Marr
Directed by: Rowan Pike
Running time: 52 minutes
Release date: October 18, at 6 a.m. Eastern time
Setting: Bellwether ferry terminal, a fictional coastal location

The episode is the fourth installment in *Harbor Lights*. It can be heard on its own; the previous installments are not required to follow Mara’s story. Earlier episodes introduced the terminal and some of its staff, but this installment centers on the night dispatcher and the final seasonal crossing. North Window Audio describes the series as an independent production and has not announced a broadcast partner for this episode.

A short listening event will take place at the East Quay Library on October 20 at 7 p.m. The event is free, and the room has space for 40 people. Pike and Marr are scheduled to attend for a discussion after the episode, subject to their availability. The library will provide a printed transcript and a captioned video presentation of the episode’s production notes; the drama itself remains an audio recording. Questions may be submitted on paper at the event or asked during the discussion. The library is at 14 Harbor Street, beside the public ferry pier. The event is not a live performance, and no additional scenes are planned.

The production began in February, when Marr submitted a five-page outline to North Window Audio’s story group. The group returned notes on the pacing of the second half and asked for a clearer reason that Mara stays at the terminal after the eastern route closes. Marr revised the outline before drafting the full script in April. Pike and the performers held one table read in June, followed by two recording sessions in August. The final mix was completed in September. The team recorded the harbor notices separately so they could adjust their position in the sound mix without changing the actors’ dialogue.

North Window Audio has scheduled no additional episodes of *Harbor Lights* for release this year. The studio’s website lists the current cast, episode transcript, and listening information, and its mailing list provides release notices. “The Last Ferry Bell” will remain available on the episode page after October 18. The production is intended for general audiences; it contains storm sounds and discussion of a dangerous crossing, but no graphic violence. could you take a look at the draft for our radio drama episode, “Room for the Tide,” and help make the wording easier to follow without making it sound too formal? it’s planned as a 28-minute episode in six scenes, set in Grayhaven, a small port town. I’m trying to keep the story intimate, even though the storm and the ferry schedule give it a fairly busy background. The main people are Mara Vale, the night dispatcher at the ferry station; Jo Pell, a volunteer archivist; and Len Ortiz, a ferry mechanic. Nessa is heard only in an old recording, and I’m not sure yet whether the audience should understand right away who she is.

The first scene begins shortly before midnight, with Mara alone in the station. The harbor warning system is being tested, not because a storm has arrived, and I want that distinction to be clear. A low tone comes through the wall speaker, then a burst of static, then the spoken test message. Mara has heard the test many times, so she shouldn’t sound frightened by it. She does notice that the final chime seems to hang in the room longer than usual. That might be the building acoustics, or it might be the first hint of the recording, but I don’t want the script to settle that question too early. The ferry is delayed by forty minutes because of a mechanical inspection, and Mara has to explain that to a caller who is waiting on the other side of the inlet.

Jo arrives carrying two archive boxes from the town reading room. One box has ferry timetables and maintenance notes from the year the old hotel closed; the other has recordings that were made for a local history project and were never catalogued properly. Jo says, “I was told this one was mostly people reading dates into a microphone.” I like the line because it makes her sound practical rather than spooky, but please check that the joke doesn’t take the tension out of the scene. She’s hoping to find a specific interview with Nessa, who worked at the hotel desk before it shut. She can’t remember whether Nessa’s surname is written on the box, and neither can Mara, so please don’t give her one.

Len comes in from the pier with wet sleeves and a clipboard. He’s checked the ferry’s engine himself, but the inspection is still ongoing, and he can’t promise when the boat will leave. He and Mara know each other well enough to speak casually, though neither of them says outright that they used to be close. Len asks whether the station speaker always makes the test chime ring twice. Mara says, “It rings once. You’re hearing the room.” The line is meant to leave it uncertain whether he really heard something extra. Please keep that uncertainty; I don’t want Len to be confirmed as right or Mara to be confirmed as right in this episode.

The middle section switches between the waiting room and the archive boxes, but the scene changes should be easy to follow in audio. We don’t have a narrator, and the listener can’t see the stage directions. I’ve used the ferry bell as a transition sound in two places, but I’m worried that it sounds like the boat is leaving when it isn’t. Could you flag any point where a sound cue gives the wrong impression about the ferry’s status? The storm is still out over the water at this point. There is rain on the station windows, but no flooding, no damage, and no evacuation. I want the weather to add pressure without turning this into a disaster story.

For the archive recording, Nessa describes a night when the hotel telephone kept ringing after the line had been disconnected. The script doesn’t establish whether that memory is true, a misunderstanding, or a story she liked to tell. Her voice should sound ordinary and a little tired, not like a ghost. The recorded line is: “If the desk lamp was on, someone was expected.” Please leave the wording of that quote exactly as it is. Jo recognizes the room number mentioned a few seconds later as the room above the old ferry office, but she isn’t certain the hotel and ferry office shared a wall. That detail is something she wants to check, not a fact she has proved.

A few things I’d especially appreciate help with:
1. Please smooth awkward dialogue and stage directions, while keeping the characters’ speech distinct. Mara is concise at work; Jo explains more when she’s thinking aloud; Len tends to answer the practical question first and the personal one later.
2. Please keep the difference between the planned warning-system test and an actual storm alert clear. The episode doesn’t include an alert.
3. Please point out any scene transition or sound cue that may confuse someone listening without a script. The old recording has a soft click before it begins, and I’d like to keep that if it reads clearly as playback starting.
4. Please note any line that makes the relationship between Mara and Len sound more definite than the draft supports. Their history is suggested, but it isn’t explained here.

At the end, the ferry is still delayed, the engine inspection hasn’t been resolved, and the storm remains offshore. Mara puts the archive recording away rather than playing it again. There’s another test chime, but the episode cuts before anyone says whether it rang once or twice. I’d like the last page to stay quiet and unresolved, without adding a new reveal.
